title: Agnostic Learnability of Halfspaces via Logistic Loss

en.text: Logistic regression is probably the most widely deployed classifier in existence: one convex objective, one call, and it is nearly everyone's first move. Yet a basic question about it stayed unsettled for a long time — when the labels are corrupted by noise, how well does logistic regression actually learn?

This ICML 2022 paper trains that question on one of the oldest objects in learning theory: agnostically learning homogeneous halfspaces. A halfspace is just a linear classifier through the origin. "Agnostic" means we let an adversary flip an OPT fraction of the labels of an otherwise perfectly linearly separable dataset, so the best any linear classifier can hope for is a zero-one error of OPT — the error of that optimal halfspace itself. The goal is to get close to OPT on the corrupted data.

Before this work, the theory sat between two bounds with a wide gap in the middle. On one side, a lower bound says no convex surrogate loss can beat Ω(OPT). On the other, the best known upper bound only guarantees logistic regression reaches Õ(√OPT). Which bound reflects the truth for logistic regression? The paper closes the gap — and, along the way, hands over a surprisingly cheap fix.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13419 (ICML 2022)
The setup: agnostically learning a halfspace

The problem is clean. We draw feature-label samples from an unknown distribution and want a linear classifier whose zero-one error is close to OPT, the smallest error achievable by any homogeneous halfspace. Equivalently, hand a perfectly separable dataset to an adversary who may flip an OPT fraction of its labels; we then try to recover the original decision boundary as closely as the corruption allows.

Logistic regression is the natural heuristic here — it minimizes a smooth convex loss, so it is easy to optimize and to analyze. The catch is its worst-case behavior, which is alarming: Ben-David et al. (2012) showed that on an adversarially constructed distribution, the logistic-risk minimizer can be wrong on nearly a 1−OPT fraction of examples. To rule out such pathologies, the field restricts attention to well-behaved distributions (isotropic log-concave ones, for instance), where much stronger guarantees hold. But even under that assumption, whether logistic regression achieves order OPT or order √OPT was open — and that gap is exactly what decides whether we can recommend it with confidence.
The bad news: logistic regression is stuck at √OPT — and it is tight

The paper's first result is a lower bound that settles which side of the gap is real: even on a well-behaved distribution, logistic regression cannot escape √OPT. The argument is not abstract — the authors build an explicit counterexample. The distribution Q below is two-dimensional, isotropic, and fully well-behaved, yet it reliably defeats logistic regression.

en.caption: Figure 1. The counterexample distribution Q the paper constructs — two-dimensional, isotropic, and well-behaved. A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. The small hatched squares Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ hold a carefully placed sliver of noisy examples: together they carry only an OPT fraction of the mass, yet they are enough to tilt the logistic-risk minimizer off the axis and force a zero-one error of order √OPT.

en.text: The whole construction is about leverage. The background Q₄ makes the distribution look tame, and the optimal boundary is plainly the vertical axis. But the little squares in the corners, though they carry almost no mass (only OPT of it), are positioned so precisely that the logistic loss over-weights them during optimization and settles on a direction pulled away from the axis. The authors prove that on this Q, the global minimizer w* of the logistic risk has zero-one error at least √OPT/(60π), for OPT small enough (the construction requires OPT ≤ 1/100). That √OPT exactly matches Frei et al.'s known Õ(√OPT) upper bound — so √OPT is the true rate for logistic regression on its own, and no analysis can do better. That is precisely what it means to close the gap.
When logistic regression already suffices: radial Lipschitzness

If the √OPT pathology comes from the density pulling unevenly at different radii, the natural question is what condition makes that pull vanish. The paper's answer is clean: radial Lipschitzness of the density. Intuitively, as long as the feature density changes gently along the radial direction, logistic regression is not dragged off course by a pocket of corner noise, and it reaches the near-optimal Õ(OPT) rate on its own.

More precisely, the upper bound reads O((1+Cκ)·OPT), where the constant Cκ is an integral of the radial-Lipschitzness modulus: the smoother the density is along the radius, the smaller Cκ, and it vanishes entirely when the density is radially symmetric. The same upper-bound argument is also notably versatile — it recovers the earlier Õ(√OPT) result as a special case, and it goes through for the hinge loss as well as the logistic loss. That last point is exactly what makes the two-phase algorithm below possible.
The cheap fix: logistic regression plus one perceptron step

Radial Lipschitzness is, after all, an extra assumption. The paper's most useful contribution is a two-phase algorithm that needs no such assumption and works for every well-behaved distribution — and it is barely more than "run logistic regression, then take one more step."

Phase one is logistic regression itself: projected gradient descent on the logistic risk inside a ball of radius 1/√ε, returning a direction v. By the analysis above, v lands within angle Õ(√OPT+ε) of the true direction ū — roughly right, but the zero-one error is still stuck at √OPT. Phase two then runs projected stochastic gradient descent on the hinge loss, whose update rule is exactly the classical perceptron: starting from the warm start v and confined to a bounded domain, it keeps sharpening. This tightens the angle and drives the zero-one error down to order OPT.

The savings are the striking part. Prior algorithms that reached O(OPT+ε) had to solve O(log(1/OPT)) minimization problems while binary-searching for OPT; this method needs just two convex steps — logistic regression plus one perceptron phase. Its sample complexity also drops from the Õ(d/ε⁴) of earlier nonconvex approaches to Õ(d/ε²), a quadratic improvement.

en.caption: Table 1. The two-phase algorithm versus prior nonconvex methods: the error rate matches, but the number of convex minimizations and the sample complexity both fall sharply.

en.text: The rates at a glance

Laid side by side, the story of where logistic regression falls short and how to patch it becomes obvious: on its own it is stuck at √OPT, but either adding radial Lipschitzness or appending one perceptron step brings it back to order OPT.

en.caption: Table 2. Zero-one error rates across settings. OPT is the best error any linear classifier can achieve; on well-behaved distributions logistic regression only reaches √OPT, a rate the paper's counterexample proves is tight.
rows: Logistic regression, general well-behaved dist. (known upper bound)
Logistic regression on the counterexample Q (this paper's lower bound)

en.text: Takeaways and boundaries

Two things are worth carrying away. First, for agnostically learning halfspaces, logistic regression on its own cannot beat √OPT, and that rate is tight — the paper corners it with an explicit well-behaved distribution. Second, the remedy is remarkably cheap: warm-start from the logistic solution, append one perceptron-style convex minimization, and the guarantee jumps to near-optimal Õ(OPT) on any well-behaved distribution, more simply and with better sample efficiency than any prior method. Along the way, the paper identifies radial Lipschitzness as the natural condition under which logistic regression already succeeds.

A note on scope: this is a theory paper. The results are theorems with explicit constants, not experimental curves, and every guarantee rests on the well-behaved family of distributions (isotropic, bounded or sub-exponential, satisfying soft-margin and regularity conditions). The distribution Q is a hand-crafted two-dimensional instance built to prove the lower bound, not real data. What the paper delivers is a sharp picture of how good logistic regression can be in principle, and the minimal step that closes the remaining gap — an intuition worth carrying back to practical noisy linear-classification tasks.

zh.text: 逻辑回归（logistic regression）大概是被部署得最多的分类算法：一行调用、一个凸优化，几乎所有人的第一反应都是它。但一个很基础的问题一直没有说清楚——当标签被噪声污染时，逻辑回归到底学得有多好？

这篇 ICML 2022 的论文把镜头对准了学习理论里最经典的对象：不可知地学习齐次半空间（agnostically learning homogeneous halfspaces）。所谓「半空间」就是一个过原点的线性分类器；所谓「不可知」，可以理解成有一个对手被允许翻转 OPT 比例的标签，把原本线性可分的数据弄脏。我们能指望的最好结果，就是把零一错误率做到 OPT 附近——也就是那个最优线性分类器本身的错误率。
在此之前，理论界对逻辑回归的评价夹在两个界之间，中间是一道很宽的缝：一方面有下界说，任何凸代理损失（convex surrogate loss）都别想比 Ω(OPT) 更好；另一方面已知的上界只保证逻辑回归能做到 Õ(√OPT)。到底哪个界才是逻辑回归的真实速率？本文把这道缝彻底合上了，并顺手给出一个便宜得惊人的修复方案。
论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13419（ICML 2022）
背景：什么叫「不可知地学半空间」
设定很干净。我们从一个未知分布里拿到一批「特征-标签」样本，目标是找一个线性分类器，让它的零一错误率尽量接近 OPT——OPT 是所有齐次半空间里能达到的最小零一错误率。等价地说，把一份本来完美线性可分的数据交给对手，允许它翻转其中 OPT 比例的标签，我们要在这份被污染的数据上尽量逼近原来的那条分界线。

逻辑回归是这里最自然的启发式做法：它最小化一个光滑的凸损失，好优化、好分析。麻烦在于它的最坏情况相当吓人——Ben-David 等人（2012）早就指出，在对手精心构造的分布上，逻辑回归的最优解可能错到 1−OPT，几乎全错。为了排除这种病态，理论界通常把注意力收缩到「良态分布」（well-behaved distributions，比如各向同性的对数凹分布）上，那里能证明强得多的保证。但即便加了这层假设，逻辑回归在良态分布上究竟是 OPT 量级还是 √OPT 量级，一直悬而未决——而这恰恰决定了我们该不该放心地推荐它。
坏消息：逻辑回归被卡在 √OPT，而且是紧的
论文的第一个结果是一个下界，回答了「哪个界是真的」这个问题：即使在良态分布上，逻辑回归也逃不出 √OPT。作者的做法不是抽象论证，而是亲手造了一个反例。下图就是这个分布 Q——一个二维、各向同性、完全满足良态条件的分布，却能稳稳地把逻辑回归难住。

zh.caption: 图1 论文构造的反例分布 Q（二维、各向同性、well-behaved）。单位圆盘上铺着一个「背景」成分 Q₄，标签由 x₁ 的符号决定（红色为 +1，蓝色为 −1），所以真正的最优半空间就是竖直的纵轴。四个带阴影的小方块 Q₁、Q₂、Q₃ 精心放置了一小撮带噪声的样本：它们合计只占 OPT 比例，却足以把逻辑回归的最优解从纵轴「拽偏」，最终逼出 √OPT 量级的零一错误。

zh.text: 图里的关键在于「杠杆」。背景 Q₄ 让整个分布看起来规规矩矩，最优分界线明明就是那条纵轴；但角落里那几个小方块虽然质量很轻（只有 OPT 那么多），位置却选得极巧，逻辑损失在优化时会被它们过度「拉扯」，最终收敛到一个偏离纵轴的方向。作者证明，在这个 Q 上，逻辑风险的全局最小解 w* 的零一错误至少是 √OPT/(60π)（当 OPT 足够小，论文的构造要求 OPT ≤ 1/100）。这个 √OPT 正好匹配 Frei 等人已知的 Õ(√OPT) 上界——也就是说，逻辑回归单打独斗时，√OPT 就是它的真实速率，一分都快不了。这就是所谓「把缝合上」的确切含义。
什么时候逻辑回归本来就够用：径向 Lipschitz 条件
既然 √OPT 的病根来自密度在不同半径上的不均匀「拉扯」，一个自然的问题是：加上什么条件能让这种拉扯消失？论文给出的答案很干净——密度的径向 Lipschitz 性（radial Lipschitzness）。直观地说，只要特征密度沿半径方向变化得足够平缓，逻辑回归就不会被角落里的小噪声带偏，它自己就能直接达到近最优的 Õ(OPT) 速率。
更精细地看，论文的上界写成 O((1+Cκ)·OPT)，其中常数 Cκ 是径向 Lipschitz 模的一个积分；密度沿半径越平滑，Cκ 越小，当密度径向对称时它直接消失。同一套上界论证还很「通用」：它既能作为特例复现出此前 Õ(√OPT) 的结论，也同样适用于 hinge 损失——最后这一点，正是下面那个两阶段算法能成立的关键。
便宜的修复：逻辑回归 +「一步感知机」
径向 Lipschitz 毕竟是个额外假设。论文最实用的贡献，是给出一个不需要任何此类假设、对所有良态分布都成立的两阶段算法，而且简单到几乎是「逻辑回归再走一步」。

第一阶段就是逻辑回归本身：在半径为 1/√ε 的球里对逻辑风险做投影梯度下降，拿到一个方向 v。由前面的分析，v 与真实方向 ū 的夹角是 Õ(√OPT+ε)——方向大致对了，但零一错误还停在 √OPT。第二阶段接着用 hinge 损失做投影随机梯度下降，其更新规则恰好就是经典的感知机（perceptron）：从 v 这个「热启动」出发，把优化限制在一个有界的区域里继续磨。这一步把夹角进一步收紧，零一错误随之被压到 OPT 量级。
省下来的代价才是真正惊人的地方。此前能做到 O(OPT+ε) 的算法，要在二分搜索 OPT 的同时求解 O(log(1/OPT)) 个最小化问题；而这里只需要两步凸优化——逻辑回归加一步感知机。样本复杂度也从此前非凸方法的 Õ(d/ε⁴) 降到 Õ(d/ε²)，是一个平方级的改进。

zh.caption: 表1 两阶段算法与此前非凸方法的对比：错误率相当，但凸优化次数与样本复杂度都大幅下降。

zh.text: 一张表看清各种速率
把上面的结果并排放在一起，逻辑回归「差在哪、怎么补」就一目了然：单靠逻辑回归卡在 √OPT；加径向 Lipschitz，或者接一步感知机，都能回到 OPT 量级。

zh.caption: 表2 不同设定下的零一错误速率。OPT 是任意线性分类器能达到的最优错误率；良态分布下逻辑回归只能到 √OPT，且这一速率被本文的反例证明是紧的。
rows: 逻辑回归，一般良态分布（已知上界）
逻辑回归在反例 Q 上（本文下界）
逻辑回归 + 径向 Lipschitz
两阶段算法，次指数分布

zh.text: 小结与边界

这篇论文留下两句可以带走的话。第一，对不可知地学半空间来说，逻辑回归自己只能到 √OPT，而且这个速率是紧的——论文用一个明确的良态分布把它逼到了墙角。第二，补救的成本低得出奇：从逻辑回归的解热启动，追加一步感知机式的凸最小化，就能在任意良态分布上把保证提升到近最优的 Õ(OPT)，比此前任何方法都更简单、样本效率也更好。顺带地，论文还点明了径向 Lipschitz 是让逻辑回归「本来就够用」的那个自然条件。
需要说明边界：这是一篇纯理论工作，结论是带明确常数的定理，而不是数据集上的实验曲线；所有保证都建立在「良态分布」这一族假设之上（各向同性、有界或次指数、满足软间隔与正则条件）。反例分布 Q 也是精心构造的二维实例，用来证明下界，而非真实数据。换句话说，它回答的是「逻辑回归在理论上能到多好、缺的那一步怎么补」，把这份直觉带回到实际的带噪线性分类任务里，往往是最有价值的读法。

逻辑回归是这里最自然的启发式做法：它最小化一个光滑的凸损失，好优化、好分析。麻烦在于它的最坏情况相当吓人——Ben-David 等人（2012）早就指出，在对手精心构造的分布上，逻辑回归的最优解可能错到 1−OPT，几乎全错。为了排除这种病态，理论界通常把注意力收缩到「良态分布」（well-behaved distributions，比如各向同性的对数凹分布）上，那里能证明强得多的保证。但即便加了这层假设，逻辑回归在良态分布上究竟是 OPT 量级还是 √OPT 量级，一直悬而未决——而这恰恰决定了我们该不该放心地推荐它。

en.subtitle: A tight √OPT lower bound — and a two-step "logistic + perceptron" fix that restores near-optimal accuracy on any well-behaved distribution. From UIUC, MIT, Google Research, and CMU.

zh.title: ICML 2022 | 逻辑回归只能解一半：不可知地学半空间到底难在哪
zh.subtitle: UIUC、MIT、Google Research、CMU 合作，证明逻辑回归被卡在 √OPT 的紧下界，并用「逻辑回归 + 一步感知机」的两阶段算法恢复近最优精度

en.caption: Figure 1. The counterexample distribution Q the paper constructs — two-dimensional, isotropic, and well-behaved. A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. The small hatched squares Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ hold a carefully placed sliver of noisy examples: together they carry only an OPT fraction of the mass, yet they are enough to tilt the logistic-risk minimizer off the axis and force a zero-one error of order √OPT.

en.text: The cheap fix: logistic regression plus one perceptron step

Radial Lipschitzness is, after all, an extra assumption. The paper's most useful contribution is a two-phase algorithm that needs no such assumption and works for every well-behaved distribution — and it is barely more than "run logistic regression, then take one more step."

Phase one is logistic regression itself: projected gradient descent on the logistic risk inside a ball of radius 1/√ε, returning a direction v. By the analysis above, v lands within angle Õ(√OPT+ε) of the true direction ū — roughly right, but the zero-one error is still stuck at √OPT. Phase two then runs projected stochastic gradient descent on the hinge loss, whose update rule is exactly the classical perceptron: starting from the warm start v and confined to a bounded domain, it keeps sharpening. This tightens the angle and drives the zero-one error down to order OPT.

The savings are the striking part. Prior algorithms that reached O(OPT+ε) had to solve O(log(1/OPT)) minimization problems while binary-searching for OPT; this method needs just two convex steps — logistic regression plus one perceptron phase. Its sample complexity also drops from the Õ(d/ε⁴) of earlier nonconvex approaches to Õ(d/ε²), a quadratic improvement.

en.caption: Table 1. The two-phase algorithm versus prior nonconvex methods: the error rate matches, but the number of convex minimizations and the sample complexity both fall sharply.

zh.caption: 图1 论文构造的反例分布 Q（二维、各向同性、well-behaved）。单位圆盘上铺着一个「背景」成分 Q₄，标签由 x₁ 的符号决定（红色为 +1，蓝色为 −1），所以真正的最优半空间就是竖直的纵轴。四个带阴影的小方块 Q₁、Q₂、Q₃ 精心放置了一小撮带噪声的样本：它们合计只占 OPT 比例，却足以把逻辑回归的最优解从纵轴「拽偏」，最终逼出 √OPT 量级的零一错误。

zh.text: 便宜的修复：逻辑回归 +「一步感知机」
径向 Lipschitz 毕竟是个额外假设。论文最实用的贡献，是给出一个不需要任何此类假设、对所有良态分布都成立的两阶段算法，而且简单到几乎是「逻辑回归再走一步」。

第一阶段就是逻辑回归本身：在半径为 1/√ε 的球里对逻辑风险做投影梯度下降，拿到一个方向 v。由前面的分析，v 与真实方向 ū 的夹角是 Õ(√OPT+ε)——方向大致对了，但零一错误还停在 √OPT。第二阶段接着用 hinge 损失做投影随机梯度下降，其更新规则恰好就是经典的感知机（perceptron）：从 v 这个「热启动」出发，把优化限制在一个有界的区域里继续磨。这一步把夹角进一步收紧，零一错误随之被压到 OPT 量级。
省下来的代价才是真正惊人的地方。此前能做到 O(OPT+ε) 的算法，要在二分搜索 OPT 的同时求解 O(log(1/OPT)) 个最小化问题；而这里只需要两步凸优化——逻辑回归加一步感知机。样本复杂度也从此前非凸方法的 Õ(d/ε⁴) 降到 Õ(d/ε²)，是一个平方级的改进。

zh.caption: 表1 两阶段算法与此前非凸方法的对比：错误率相当，但凸优化次数与样本复杂度都大幅下降。

en.text: The setup: agnostically learning a halfspace

The problem is clean. We draw feature-label samples from an unknown distribution and want a linear classifier whose zero-one error is close to OPT, the smallest error achievable by any homogeneous halfspace. Equivalently, hand a perfectly separable dataset to an adversary who may flip an OPT fraction of its labels; we then try to recover the original decision boundary as closely as the corruption allows.

Logistic regression is the natural heuristic here — it minimizes a smooth convex loss, so it is easy to optimize and to analyze. The catch is its worst-case behavior, which is alarming: Ben-David et al. (2012) showed that on an adversarially constructed distribution, the logistic-risk minimizer can be wrong on nearly a 1−OPT fraction of examples. To rule out such pathologies, the field restricts attention to well-behaved distributions (isotropic log-concave ones, for instance), where much stronger guarantees hold. But even under that assumption, whether logistic regression achieves order OPT or order √OPT was open — and that gap is exactly what decides whether we can recommend it with confidence.
The bad news: logistic regression is stuck at √OPT — and it is tight

The paper's first result is a lower bound that settles which side of the gap is real: even on a well-behaved distribution, logistic regression cannot escape √OPT. The argument is not abstract — the authors build an explicit counterexample. The distribution Q below is two-dimensional, isotropic, and fully well-behaved, yet it reliably defeats logistic regression.

en.caption: Figure 1. The counterexample distribution Q the paper constructs — two-dimensional, isotropic, and well-behaved. A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. The small hatched squares Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ hold a carefully placed sliver of noisy examples: together they carry only an OPT fraction of the mass, yet they are enough to tilt the logistic-risk minimizer off the axis and force a zero-one error of order √OPT.

en.text: The whole construction is about leverage. The background Q₄ makes the distribution look tame, and the optimal boundary is plainly the vertical axis. But the little squares in the corners, though they carry almost no mass (only OPT of it), are positioned so precisely that the logistic loss over-weights them during optimization and settles on a direction pulled away from the axis. The authors prove that on this Q, the global minimizer w* of the logistic risk has zero-one error at least √OPT/(60π), for OPT small enough (the construction requires OPT ≤ 1/100). That √OPT exactly matches Frei et al.'s known Õ(√OPT) upper bound — so √OPT is the true rate for logistic regression on its own, and no analysis can do better. That is precisely what it means to close the gap.

A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. en.text: Logistic regression is probably the most widely deployed classifier in existence: one convex objective, one call, and it is nearly everyone's first move. Yet a basic question about it stayed unsettled for a long time — when the labels are corrupted by noise, how well does logistic regression actually learn?

This ICML 2022 paper trains that question on one of the oldest objects in learning theory: agnostically learning homogeneous halfspaces. A halfspace is just a linear classifier through the origin. "Agnostic" means we let an adversary flip an OPT fraction of the labels of an otherwise perfectly linearly separable dataset, so the best any linear classifier can hope for is a zero-one error of OPT — the error of that optimal halfspace itself. The goal is to get close to OPT on the corrupted data.

Before this work, the theory sat between two bounds with a wide gap in the middle. On one side, a lower bound says no convex surrogate loss can beat Ω(OPT). On the other, the best known upper bound only guarantees logistic regression reaches Õ(√OPT). Which bound reflects the truth for logistic regression? The paper closes the gap — and, along the way, hands over a surprisingly cheap fix.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13419 (ICML 2022)

en.caption: Figure 1. The counterexample distribution Q the paper constructs — two-dimensional, isotropic, and well-behaved. A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. When logistic regression already suffices: radial Lipschitzness

If the √OPT pathology comes from the density pulling unevenly at different radii, the natural question is what condition makes that pull vanish. The paper's answer is clean: radial Lipschitzness of the density. Intuitively, as long as the feature density changes gently along the radial direction, logistic regression is not dragged off course by a pocket of corner noise, and it reaches the near-optimal Õ(OPT) rate on its own.

More precisely, the upper bound reads O((1+Cκ)·OPT), where the constant Cκ is an integral of the radial-Lipschitzness modulus: the smoother the density is along the radius, the smaller Cκ, and it vanishes entirely when the density is radially symmetric. The same upper-bound argument is also notably versatile — it recovers the earlier Õ(√OPT) result as a special case, and it goes through for the hinge loss as well as the logistic loss. That last point is exactly what makes the two-phase algorithm below possible.

zh.text: 逻辑回归（logistic regression）大概是被部署得最多的分类算法：一行调用、一个凸优化，几乎所有人的第一反应都是它。但一个很基础的问题一直没有说清楚——当标签被噪声污染时，逻辑回归到底学得有多好？

这篇 ICML 2022 的论文把镜头对准了学习理论里最经典的对象：不可知地学习齐次半空间（agnostically learning homogeneous halfspaces）。所谓「半空间」就是一个过原点的线性分类器；所谓「不可知」，可以理解成有一个对手被允许翻转 OPT 比例的标签，把原本线性可分的数据弄脏。我们能指望的最好结果，就是把零一错误率做到 OPT 附近——也就是那个最优线性分类器本身的错误率。
在此之前，理论界对逻辑回归的评价夹在两个界之间，中间是一道很宽的缝：一方面有下界说，任何凸代理损失（convex surrogate loss）都别想比 Ω(OPT) 更好；另一方面已知的上界只保证逻辑回归能做到 Õ(√OPT)。到底哪个界才是逻辑回归的真实速率？本文把这道缝彻底合上了，并顺手给出一个便宜得惊人的修复方案。
论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13419（ICML 2022）
坏消息：逻辑回归被卡在 √OPT，而且是紧的
论文的第一个结果是一个下界，回答了「哪个界是真的」这个问题：即使在良态分布上，逻辑回归也逃不出 √OPT。作者的做法不是抽象论证，而是亲手造了一个反例。下图就是这个分布 Q——一个二维、各向同性、完全满足良态条件的分布，却能稳稳地把逻辑回归难住。

zh.caption: 图1 论文构造的反例分布 Q（二维、各向同性、well-behaved）。单位圆盘上铺着一个「背景」成分 Q₄，标签由 x₁ 的符号决定（红色为 +1，蓝色为 −1），所以真正的最优半空间就是竖直的纵轴。四个带阴影的小方块 Q₁、Q₂、Q₃ 精心放置了一小撮带噪声的样本：它们合计只占 OPT 比例，却足以把逻辑回归的最优解从纵轴「拽偏」，最终逼出 √OPT 量级的零一错误。

zh.text: 图里的关键在于「杠杆」。背景 Q₄ 让整个分布看起来规规矩矩，最优分界线明明就是那条纵轴；但角落里那几个小方块虽然质量很轻（只有 OPT 那么多），位置却选得极巧，逻辑损失在优化时会被它们过度「拉扯」，最终收敛到一个偏离纵轴的方向。作者证明，在这个 Q 上，逻辑风险的全局最小解 w* 的零一错误至少是 √OPT/(60π)（当 OPT 足够小，论文的构造要求 OPT ≤ 1/100）。这个 √OPT 正好匹配 Frei 等人已知的 Õ(√OPT) 上界——也就是说，逻辑回归单打独斗时，√OPT 就是它的真实速率，一分都快不了。这就是所谓「把缝合上」的确切含义。

zh.caption: 图1 论文构造的反例分布 Q（二维、各向同性、well-behaved）。单位圆盘上铺着一个「背景」成分 Q₄，标签由 x₁ 的符号决定（红色为 +1，蓝色为 −1），所以真正的最优半空间就是竖直的纵轴。四个带阴影的小方块 Q₁、Q₂、Q₃ 精心放置了一小撮带噪声的样本：它们合计只占 OPT 比例，却足以把逻辑回归的最优解从纵轴「拽偏」，最终逼出 √OPT 量级的零一错误。

zh.text: 便宜的修复：逻辑回归 +「一步感知机」
径向 Lipschitz 毕竟是个额外假设。论文最实用的贡献，是给出一个不需要任何此类假设、对所有良态分布都成立的两阶段算法，而且简单到几乎是「逻辑回归再走一步」。

第一阶段就是逻辑回归本身：在半径为 1/√ε 的球里对逻辑风险做投影梯度下降，拿到一个方向 v。由前面的分析，v 与真实方向 ū 的夹角是 Õ(√OPT+ε)——方向大致对了，但零一错误还停在 √OPT。第二阶段接着用 hinge 损失做投影随机梯度下降，其更新规则恰好就是经典的感知机（perceptron）：从 v 这个「热启动」出发，把优化限制在一个有界的区域里继续磨。这一步把夹角进一步收紧，零一错误随之被压到 OPT 量级。
省下来的代价才是真正惊人的地方。此前能做到 O(OPT+ε) 的算法，要在二分搜索 OPT 的同时求解 O(log(1/OPT)) 个最小化问题；而这里只需要两步凸优化——逻辑回归加一步感知机。样本复杂度也从此前非凸方法的 Õ(d/ε⁴) 降到 Õ(d/ε²)，是一个平方级的改进。

en.title: ICML 2022: Logistic Regression Is Only Half the Answer for Learning Halfspaces
en.subtitle: A tight √OPT lower bound — and a two-step "logistic + perceptron" fix that restores near-optimal accuracy on any well-behaved distribution. From UIUC, MIT, Google Research, and CMU.

zh.title: ICML 2022 | 逻辑回归只能解一半：不可知地学半空间到底难在哪
zh.subtitle: UIUC、MIT、Google Research、CMU 合作，证明逻辑回归被卡在 √OPT 的紧下界，并用「逻辑回归 + 一步感知机」的两阶段算法恢复近最优精度

en.caption: Figure 1. The counterexample distribution Q the paper constructs — two-dimensional, isotropic, and well-behaved. A background component Q₄ fills the unit disk, with labels set by the sign of x₁ (red = +1, blue = −1), so the truly optimal halfspace is the vertical axis. The small hatched squares Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ hold a carefully placed sliver of noisy examples: together they carry only an OPT fraction of the mass, yet they are enough to tilt the logistic-risk minimizer off the axis and force a zero-one error of order √OPT.

en.text: The cheap fix: logistic regression plus one perceptron step

Radial Lipschitzness is, after all, an extra assumption. The paper's most useful contribution is a two-phase algorithm that needs no such assumption and works for every well-behaved distribution — and it is barely more than "run logistic regression, then take one more step."

Phase one is logistic regression itself: projected gradient descent on the logistic risk inside a ball of radius 1/√ε, returning a direction v. By the analysis above, v lands within angle Õ(√OPT+ε) of the true direction ū — roughly right, but the zero-one error is still stuck at √OPT. Phase two then runs projected stochastic gradient descent on the hinge loss, whose update rule is exactly the classical perceptron: starting from the warm start v and confined to a bounded domain, it keeps sharpening. This tightens the angle and drives the zero-one error down to order OPT.

The savings are the striking part. Prior algorithms that reached O(OPT+ε) had to solve O(log(1/OPT)) minimization problems while binary-searching for OPT; this method needs just two convex steps — logistic regression plus one perceptron phase. Its sample complexity also drops from the Õ(d/ε⁴) of earlier nonconvex approaches to Õ(d/ε²), a quadratic improvement.

zh.text: 小结与边界

这篇论文留下两句可以带走的话。第一，对不可知地学半空间来说，逻辑回归自己只能到 √OPT，而且这个速率是紧的——论文用一个明确的良态分布把它逼到了墙角。第二，补救的成本低得出奇：从逻辑回归的解热启动，追加一步感知机式的凸最小化，就能在任意良态分布上把保证提升到近最优的 Õ(OPT)，比此前任何方法都更简单、样本效率也更好。顺带地，论文还点明了径向 Lipschitz 是让逻辑回归「本来就够用」的那个自然条件。
需要说明边界：这是一篇纯理论工作，结论是带明确常数的定理，而不是数据集上的实验曲线；所有保证都建立在「良态分布」这一族假设之上（各向同性、有界或次指数、满足软间隔与正则条件）。反例分布 Q 也是精心构造的二维实例，用来证明下界，而非真实数据。换句话说，它回答的是「逻辑回归在理论上能到多好、缺的那一步怎么补」，把这份直觉带回到实际的带噪线性分类任务里，往往是最有价值的读法。

en.text: Takeaways and boundaries

Two things are worth carrying away. First, for agnostically learning halfspaces, logistic regression on its own cannot beat √OPT, and that rate is tight — the paper corners it with an explicit well-behaved distribution. Second, the remedy is remarkably cheap: warm-start from the logistic solution, append one perceptron-style convex minimization, and the guarantee jumps to near-optimal Õ(OPT) on any well-behaved distribution, more simply and with better sample efficiency than any prior method. Along the way, the paper identifies radial Lipschitzness as the natural condition under which logistic regression already succeeds.

A note on scope: this is a theory paper. The results are theorems with explicit constants, not experimental curves, and every guarantee rests on the well-behaved family of distributions (isotropic, bounded or sub-exponential, satisfying soft-margin and regularity conditions). The distribution Q is a hand-crafted two-dimensional instance built to prove the lower bound, not real data. What the paper delivers is a sharp picture of how good logistic regression can be in principle, and the minimal step that closes the remaining gap — an intuition worth carrying back to practical noisy linear-classification tasks.

更精细地看，论文的上界写成 O((1+Cκ)·OPT)，其中常数 Cκ 是径向 Lipschitz 模的一个积分；密度沿半径越平滑，Cκ 越小，当密度径向对称时它直接消失。同一套上界论证还很「通用」：它既能作为特例复现出此前 Õ(√OPT) 的结论，也同样适用于 hinge 损失——最后这一点，正是下面那个两阶段算法能成立的关键。
